### 2026-10-28: # October 27 and 28: Designing the Schematic

**3h**

# October 27 and 28: Designing the Schematic

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.19.01 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/8e2c38d64131d6c350c1fce737f84a018de1860b22b4a419561f3b11d231027b.png)

This week I'll be designing a virtual sandbox, a simple fidget toy where each pixel on an OLED screen represents a grain of sand, and you can move it around through motion. Before actually starting, I had an idea for how I would go about designing this project. I would use the classic 0.96" OLED screen and make sure it is single-colored for uniformity. I also needed an accelerometer to track the motion, so I decided on the LIS3DH. It's relatively cheap, small enough for the project, and has lots of documentation online so I can learn how to program it. For the microcontroller, I'm using the ESP32-S3, the same chip I used in my Bee Board project from last week. I already have some experience with it, so that should make designing just a little bit easier.

For the schematic, I first added the chip, then I added a 1x4 generic connector to represent the OLED and a 1x8 connector to represent the accelerometer. I searched up the order of pins of each component and considered the orientation I want to make sure I wire the parts correctly. Then, I added a button, but I'm not too sure what I'll do with it yet. I'm considering making it a reset button, or maybe even something that changes the mode.

After finding and adding all the footprints, I still felt like something was missing, and then I realized that I should make the sandbox portable. I thought that I would have to rethink my entire project, but it turns out that the bottom of my board actually has some solder pads for a battery. I had learn a little bit about batteries as I went because this is the first project that I'm working with them.

I thought that it would be kind of impractical to have a device that's constantly on, so I added a toggle switch so I can shut it off whenever I like. I'm pretty proud of the way I did this: I added a 1x1 connector for the  battery's positive wire to go in, and that leads to the toggle switch on the PCB, and that leads to another 1x1 connector where I can attach another wire that'll go directly to the solder pad on the ESP32. By making it like this, the switch can be fixed in place.

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.19.39 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/d3d5cbe4adb842f00018ceae0fb4096984221728cff37c1bb21871a667a2a901.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 at 5.20.50 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/828fb4739999647a86b38ed4519cdd8044f011368d50d9d8151e9191996c1f1a.png)

There's a big problem that needs fixing when I design my PCB though. The battery pads are on the other side of the board, so I won't be able to access them if I lay the ESP32 flush against the PCB. I'm debating between two solutions: adding a cutout on the PCB itself, or finding a way to raise the board so that I can access it from below.

Next I'll work on that, and then after I'll tackle the firmware.

# tl;dr: I finished designing the schematic for my virtual sandbox. I added the connectors for the OLED and accelerometer, and later I decided to add a battery and a toggle switch. I had to do some research on how to do this. I came up with a good solution to mount the switch on the PCB and have wires that go in/out of 1x1 connectors. I need to find out a way for me to connect the battery wires to the underside of the microcontroller, which is what I plan to tackle next.

### 2026-10-30: # October 28-29: Designing the PCB

**4.5h**

# October 28-29: Designing the PCB

![Screenshot 2026-10-30 at 3.22.21 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/5f860eade22944150cbb6bae70e249b58922307f45ad5279244dd42770976966.png)

With the schematic done, I moved on to making the PCB. My goal was to make a compact stack, with the screen and button on the front and the ESP32, accelerometer, battery, and on/off switch on the back. I set the board outline at 32x52mm, which is big enough for the all the components on the back to fit nicely. The front is still spacious and clean, which makes the final product look like something professionally made.

Firstly, I placed the OLED. I searched up what the dimensions of a 0.96" screen are and drew a rectangle to represent that. Then, using that as reference, I placed the OLED's 1x4 connector in an appropriate spot. I decided to put the pins at the bottom so that the traces flow nicer. Next, I put the button just below the screen, where your thumb would go if you're holding the device.

![Screenshot 2026-10-30 at 3.20.32 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/d071f065dd55de82fd87d2aebda1514e29093321ce4a7bf3aaaf0acb6c6f3b73.png)

Next, I added the components to the back. I added the accelerometer using the same method I used for the OLED: drawing a rectangle to get an idea for where I should put the connector. I found that it fit nicely towards the bottom of the board, so that's where I put it. I added the ESP32 on the top-center for a clean symmetrical look and and easy point of access for charging. I also left some extra space to put the battery. I still need to figure out how I should attach it to the board though, because I wasn't planning on making an entire case.

![Screenshot 2026-10-30 at 3.21.29 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/05b09e7db27ae46e42ba221c0a8074ac438414b1cfb2648605ee1d69b3da550f.png)

I still needed to address the battery problem from last time. The battery solder pads are on the underside of the ESP32, so if it sits flush on the PCB, I wouldn't be able to reach them. I was debating between two solutions: cutting a hole in the board, or using header pins to raise the board so I can feed the wires through the gaps. I initially tried cutting a hole, which I had to research how to do, and it took a couple attempts to get a hole that looked right. Then I realized I made a pretty silly mistake. The OLED screen would be covering the hole, giving me the same problem I was trying to solve! I ultimately decided to just use header pins for the ESP32 to raise it and feed the wires through the gaps. Looking back, it would've probably been better to start with this because it would make assembly a lot easier when it comes time to do that.

![Screenshot 2026-10-30 at 3.23.24 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/bd63c39b0c2186d8c5410d4d0579c5af428522184c995d7c324b89ea4ef8cc01.png)

Routing was kind of annoying because I kept restarting to get it the way I liked it. I tried to "weave" the traces on the front and back so that they easily mesh together without crossing or making those ugly super long traces. After finishing, I ran the DRC to check everything. It was giving me some errors about the silkscreen text overlapping pads, so I made some small modifications until the DRC read zero errors.

![Screenshot 2026-10-30 at 3.24.24 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/e4c5ec3feca5cb0a9fd7436c4d335afd495d1cda70bc0e10d0605ca147371618.png)

To finish up, I rounded the corners to make the device nicer to hold, and added my name on the back.

I'm pretty happy with the finished product, and now I'll move on to the firmware.

# tl;dr: I designed the PCB for the virtual sandbox as a two-sided stack. The OLED and button are on the front, and the ESP32, accelerometer, and power switch are on the back. To get to the battery pads under the ESP32, I mounted it on headers instead of cutting a hole in the board. Then I routed the board and fixed the DRC errors.

### 2026-11-01: # October 31: Testing and Finalizing Firmware

**4h**

# October 31: Testing and Finalizing Firmware

The last big thing I needed to do was make the firmware. Since I don't have the parts yet, I couldn't test anything on the actual board. Instead of writing all the code blindly, I mocked up a quick prototype on a breadboard using an Arduino Nano and an MPU9250.

I quickly realized that the Nano simply wasn't powerful enough to handle the graphics for the sand particles, so I switched to an ESP32 DevKit V1 I had used for another project. While troubleshooting, I found out that a Nano only has 2KB of RAM, and the screen alone takes up 1KB, so it could barely handle sand particles. I probably should have just started with an ESP32 because it's a lot more powerful and more similar to the board I'm actually going to use for the project.

![IMG_4414](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/b2726b91f8791726ea6b90703e76ddd9e16c8bbc60bdbb82401fd555afec4e32.jpg)

I wired an OLED screen and the MPU9250 to the I2C pins on the ESP32 and powered both using 3.3V. For the sand physics, I found a great library made by AdaFruit called PixelDust that was pretty much made for projects similar to mine. I started off with just 1000 grains of sand, but I decided that I'll try to bump it up later.

The first time I ran the code, the sand was moving, but in the wrong directions, so I traced the error to a problem with the MPU9250's orientation compared to the screen. When I tilted the breadboard down, the sand went left. When I tilted it right, the sand went up. It took me a bit to figure out, but the accelerometer's X and Y axes were rotated 90 degrees compared to the screen, and one of them was also backwards. I added three settings at the top of the code (swap X and Y, flip X, flip Y) so I could fix it without touching the rest of the program. After a few uploads, the sand finally poured toward whichever side was lowest. Once that worked, I bumped it up to 2000 grains, and the ESP32 had no trouble keeping up.

![IMG_4415](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/1696f67290d9dba842c6dde6f69608a76f3696763190311cba4387a13901c163.jpg)

![Screenshot 2026-11-01 at 12.39.13 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/7ad5695f9c91888d80c2b646454b832c8f07cc9a727f98ec0ca4d12aa64945ae.png)

After I got a solid prototype working, I moved everything over to the real hardware I'll be using on the PCB: ESP32-S3, the LIS3DH, and the button. I switched out the MPU9250's code for code I wrote using the LIS3DH library and changed the I2C address. I rotated the screen 180 degrees because on my PCB, the screen is oriented with the pins at the bottom and not the top.

The last step was deciding what the button will do. I initially wanted it to make the device enter sleep mode, but I felt that it would be impractical because there's already an on/off switch. Instead, I set it to change the amount of grains of sand there are. It can be set to 250, 500, 1000, 2000, or 3000 grains of sand. Since PixelDust can't change the number of grains after it's been created, I had to work with pointers for the first time so that you can simply delete a sandbox from memory and build a new one when a different grain amount is made.

![Screenshot 2026-11-01 at 12.39.41 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/oWK9iPLBGiJtrZ5WPQtAnBOy06yuxWnK/8fd23af00397282a00419580db5c86e739abb411d8fa57082cd27ebc8a7d3308.png)

The final touches I still need to make are finishing the GitHub repo and finding parts.

# tl;dr: I wrote the firmware for virtual sandbox. I initially tested on hardware I already have (MPU9250, ESP32 DevKit V1, Arduino Nano) before revising the code so that it works with the hardware I'm actually going to use. I decided to make the button switch the amount of grains that are displayed on screen.
